bib.title: SliceGPT: Compress Large Language Models by Deleting Rows and Columns

question: Can a trained LLM be compressed post hoc by replacing each weight matrix with a smaller dense one (reducing embedding dimension) while keeping accuracy and getting real speedups?
hypothesis: An orthogonal change of basis per block lets the signal be projected onto its principal components so minor ones can be sliced away with little loss.
contributions: Computational invariance: orthogonal transforms can be applied to each weight matrix in a transformer without changing the model.
Per-block PCA projection of the signal between blocks, then deleting rows/columns (SliceGPT).
Experiments on OPT and LLAMA-2 (and Phi-2 zero-shot) up to 30% slicing, with superior perplexity to SparseGPT 2:4.

method.summary: Convert LayerNorm to RMSNorm, compute a per-block orthogonal matrix Q from PCA of calibration activations (eigenvectors of sum X^T X, double precision), insert Q^T_l Q_{l+1} in residual connections, and delete the minor columns/rows. Optional LoRA recovery fine-tuning.
method.task: post-training structured compression of decoder-only LLMs

datasets.name: WikiText-2 train
datasets.split: calibration from training set; perplexity on WikiText-2 test (inferred)

training.objective: inferred: LoRA recovery fine-tuning (objective not stated)

other.rft_data: approximately 1k sequences for WikiText-2-sliced models, 5k for Alpaca-sliced
other.rft_not_applied: no RFT params found that improved OPT models
other.pca_precision: double (FP32 degrades larger models, Appendix A.2)

inference.samples: single run per config; no seeds or variance reported
inference.prompting: zero-shot via LM Evaluation Harness defaults

parameters.throughput_protocol: seq len 128, batch doubled until OOM or drop-off, 80GB H100
parameters.latency_protocol: batch size 1, 128-token generation, A100 40GB and Quadro RTX6000 24GB
parameters.matmul_timing: seq len 2048, A100 80GB, cuSparseLt 0.5, median over 103 runs

metrics.name: Mean zero-shot accuracy
metrics.definition: average over PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c

metrics.name: Per-token latency / GPUms
metrics.definition: ms per token times number of GPUs

eval.protocol: Single runs; no seeds or error bars stated.

evidence.quote: For all RFT we use lora_r = 32, lora_alpha = 10 and sequence length 1024

results.claim: Without recovery fine-tuning, slicing 25% of parameters keeps 99% (OPT 66B), 96% (LLAMA-2 70B) and 87% (Phi-2) of dense zero-shot accuracy.
results.setup: Mean of PIQA, WinoGrande, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c via LM Evaluation Harness; no RFT; Section 5 conclusion. Abstract states 99%, 99%, 90% for the same models without saying the latter two need RFT.
results.note: Abstract prints 99%, 99% and 90% for LLAMA-2 70B, OPT 66B, Phi-2; conclusion gives 99%, 96%, 87% without RFT and 99% (LLAMA-2 70B), 90% (Phi-2) with RFT. Per Table 8 (Alpaca calibration) LLAMA-2 70B 25%: 73.59 vs dense 76.57; with WikiText-2 calibration (Table 7) 69.75.
results.quote: slicing OPT 66B, LLAMA-2 70B and Phi-2 at 25% maintains 99%, 96% and 87% of the dense performance

results.claim: With LoRA recovery fine-tuning on Alpaca, 25%-sliced LLAMA-2 70B and Phi-2 recover to 99% and 90% of dense performance.
results.setup: Alpaca calibration and Alpaca RFT, LoRA r=32, 5k sequences, 25% slicing.
results.quote: With recovery fine-tuning 25%-sliced LLAMA-2 70B and Phi-2 increase to 99% and 90% respectively.

results.claim: LLAMA-2 70B sliced 30% with Alpaca RFT averages 74.3% against 76.6% dense.
results.setup: 30% slice (~51.6B params), Alpaca calibration plus RFT, five zero-shot tasks.
results.quote: we are able to achieve an average accuracy of 74.3%, compared to 76.6% on the dense model

results.claim: Phi-2 at 25% slicing with RFT averages 65.2% vs 72.2% dense (90.3% retained).
results.setup: Alpaca calibration and RFT; sliced model ~2.2B params vs 2.8B.
results.quote: The average accuracy of Phi-2 with 25% slicing and RFT is 65.2%, compared to 72.2% with the dense model.

results.claim: 25%-sliced models reach up to 1.55x token throughput over dense on 80GB H100s (LLAMA-2 70B); other 25% cases are 1.06x-1.13x.
results.setup: Sequence length 128; batch size doubled until OOM or throughput drops; Table 11: LLAMA-2 70B dense 541 tok/s at batch 128 on 2 GPUs, 25% sliced 839 tok/s at batch 256 on 2 GPUs (sliced model fits a larger batch).
results.note: Throughput at max batch, not latency; OPT 13B 1.13x, OPT 66B 1.08x, LLAMA-2 13B 1.06x at 25%.
results.quote: The 25% sliced models achieve up to 1.55× throughput improvement over the dense model.

results.claim: At 50% slicing the two largest models fit on one GPU instead of two, giving 3.13x and 1.87x throughput (6.26x and 3.75x for a fixed GPU count).
results.setup: H100 80GB, sequence length 128, OPT 66B and LLAMA-2 70B.
results.note: Table 11 prints 6.26x and 3.75x for 1 GPU vs dense on 2 GPUs.
results.quote: At 50% slicing the largest models require only one GPU instead of two, with large increases in throughput: 3.13× and 1.87×.

results.claim: LLAMA-2 70B per-token generation compute on Quadro RTX6000 falls from 1764 GPUms to 1075 GPUms (64%).
results.setup: Batch size 1, generating length-128 sequences, 25% slicing, 7 GPUs to 5 GPUs, Hugging Face code without continuous batching or sharding.
results.quote: the compute required using RTX6000 GPUs is reduced to 64%, from 1764 GPUms to 1075 GPUms

results.claim: Latency speedup at 25% slicing is 16-17% on RTX6000 and 11-13% on A100.
results.setup: OPT 66B and LLAMA-2 70B, batch size 1, 128 tokens.
results.quote: We observe a speedup of 16-17% on RTX6000 GPUs when employing 25% slicing, and 11-13% on A100s.

results.claim: On 40GB A100s, inference cost of LLAMA-2 70B is reduced to 66% of dense (4 to 3 GPUs).
results.setup: Table 2: 500 GPUms dense vs 330 GPUms at 25% slicing.
results.quote: reduce the cost of inference of LLAMA-2 70B on 40GB A100 GPUs to 66% of that of the dense model

results.claim: SparseGPT 2:4 is worse than SliceGPT 25% on all LLAMA-2 sizes; for OPT, 30% sliced beats 2:4 except at 2.7B.
results.setup: LLAMA-2 70B, WikiText-2 calibration, set size 1024, seq len 2048.
results.quote: SparseGPT 2:4 performs worse than SliceGPT with 25% slicing in all LLAMA-2 models.

results.claim: At 50% slicing WikiText-2 perplexity is worse than SparseGPT 2:4 though throughput is much higher.
results.quote: We note that the WikiText2 perplexity of SliceGPT at 50% is worse than SparseGPT 2:4

results.claim: Matmul timing (A100, seq 2048): SliceGPT 25% matches SparseGPT 2:4 speedup on LLAMA-2 70B (1.32x) with better perplexity; on 7B/13B 2:4 is faster (1.48x/1.50x vs 1.33x/1.30x).
results.setup: cuSparseLt 0.5 vs PyTorch dense, median over 103 runs, per-layer matmuls only.
results.table: Table 12, rows LLAMA-2 70B SparseGPT 2:4 and SliceGPT (25%), column Total in ms (speedup)

results.claim: Single-precision PCA hurts larger models: LLAMA-2 70B at 25% is 7.01 with FP32 PCA vs 4.89 with double precision (calibration 128).
results.table: Table 4 row SliceGPT 25% col LLAMA-2 70B 7.01; Table 5 row SliceGPT (25%) 4.89

results.claim: Slicing a model costs 1-3 hours on one GPU; 3h31m for LLAMA-2 70B on 1xH100 at 30%, 5h06m total with RFT.
results.setup: Table 3: 30% slicing, Alpaca calibration 1024 sequences of 2048; RFT on 4xH100.
results.note: Text says 1 to 3 hours but Table 3 shows 3h31m for 70B; Section 4 says approximately 3.5 hours for Q on LLAMA-2 70B.
results.quote: All LLAMA-2 , OPT and Phi-2 models can be sliced on a single GPU in 1 to 3 hours.

results.claim: Varying slicing by layer helps OPT but hurts LLAMA-2 perplexity.
results.quote: Varying the slicing level by layer improves the WikiText-2 perplexity in OPT models, but has the opposite effect in LLAMA-2 models.

results.claim: Alpaca calibration/RFT gives much better zero-shot accuracy than WikiText-2, attributed to similarity to benchmark tasks.
results.quote: We attribute this difference to the similarity between Alpaca and the benchmark tasks.

results.claim: Computational invariance: RMSNorm(XQ)Q^T = RMSNorm(X), so orthogonal transforms can be folded into weights without changing outputs.
results.setup: RMSNorm-connected transformers; LayerNorm models are converted first.

results.claim: Column-norm pruning baseline failed: perplexity soared into the 1000s after pruning a few columns.
results.setup: Initial baseline pruning smallest-norm columns; no numbers given.
results.quote: WikiText-2 perplexity of the model soaring into the 1000s after pruning just a few columns

results.claim: Smaller dense LMs outperform 13B-or-smaller models pruned to similar size.
results.quote: Smaller but dense LMs perform better than LMs with 13B parameters or less pruned to similar sizes

limits: Dense smaller LMs beat 13B-or-smaller models pruned to similar size (Section 5).
Sliced models have more parameters than SparseGPT 2:4 models; at 50% slicing perplexity is worse than 2:4.
RFT could not improve OPT models.
End-to-end SparseGPT 2:4 speedups were not feasible; comparison is per-layer matmul timing only.
Latency tests used Hugging Face code without continuous batching or sharding; OPT 175B excluded.
Not combined with quantization; authors suggest it as future work.

terms.definition: it is possible to apply an orthogonal transformation to the output of one component, so long as it is undone in the next

lineage.note: structured pruning; RFT with LoRA follows it

figures.caption: Matrix multiplication of the signal X and a weight matrix W under unstructured, 2:4 and slicing sparsity
figures.why: Shows that slicing shrinks X too.

figures.caption: Computational-invariance applied per block with Q^T_l Q_{l+1} in the skip connection

problems: Table 1 and text report calibration size 1024; Table 12 LLAMA-2 70B SliceGPT 25% 12.20 total equals SparseGPT 2:4 total.
